Q: question at / pivot and >> 2 in C++ Solution for Next Higher Number A:

This solution is a combination of purely arithmetic operations (binary addition with carry) and purely bitwise manipulations.

int pivot = n & -n;

Here we get the rightmost set bit. The operation is valid only for representing negative numbers with 2's complement. I'll try to explain this:

-n = ~n + 1

If n has 1 or more zero rightmost bits, then after inversion (~) they will be set to 1. Then, after addition (+ 1), they will become zero again, and the next zero bit will be set. The remaining high bits will be reset by operation &. (There is also another explanation here.)

Why do we need this pivot number? The fact is that if we add any number from 1 to pivot - 1 to n, the number of set bits will only increase, because this addition operation will affect only the rightmost zero bits, and will not affect the remaining bits. That is, n + pivot is the minimum possible value.

Next, it will be easier to explain using a specific example: Next, it will be easier to explain using a specific example: Let n = 0b10111000. Let's highlight 3 ranges in the binary representation of this number:

CC BBB AAA
10 111 000

Where A is the rightmost zero bits. B - the nonzero bits following them, C - the remaining bits. Of course, 1 or 2 of these ranges may be empty.

            CC BBB AAA

n         = 10 111 000
pivot     = 00 001 000
n + pivot = 11 000 000

After adding n + pivot, the bits of range B are reset to zero, and the rightmost one bit of range C is set. Range B contains the quantity of bits that must be added to the sum n + pivot minus 1 bit (carried over to the range C) to get the desired number.

n ^ (n + pivot)

The xor (^) operation highlights the changes and resets the untouched bits. That is, it highlights range B and the rightmost 1 bit of range C:

                  CC BBB AAA

n               = 10 111 000
n + pivot       = 11 000 000
n ^ (n + pivot) = 01 111 000

In other words, the number n ^ (n + pivot) contains as many set bits as there are in the range B (see above) plus 1 bit carried over to the range C. It turns out that this number contains 2 more bits than we need.

To get the next number containing the same quantity of bits as n, we need to find the minimum number containing the required quantity of set bits and place it in the range A of the sum (n + pivot). To do this, we need to get rid of the rightmost zero bits in the number n ^ (n + pivot):

                            CC BBB AAA

pivot                     = 00 001 000
(n ^ (n + pivot))         = 01 111 000
(n ^ (n + pivot)) / pivot = 00 001 111

Division / pivot can be represented as / (2^m) or >> m, where m is the quantity of right shifts (equal to the quantity of rightmost zero bits).

Now we need to get rid of the 2 bits that were mentioned above. To do this, we make 2 more right shifts:

 (n ^ (n + pivot)) / pivot       = 00 001 111
((n ^ (n + pivot)) / pivot) >> 2 = 00 000 011   (= before)

All that's left is to combine the result using + or |:

                       CC BBB AAA

n + pivot            = 11 000 000
brfore               = 00 000 011
(n + pivot) | before = 11 000 011

Q: How to resume review process after updating pull request at GitHub? A:

Update August 2026:

As noted by Always a Newb at Something in the comments (comment picture), the restriction I mentioned in early 2019 no longer seems to apply, at least through the GitHub web UI, to re-requesting a review from someone who has already reviewed the pull request.

I think that GitHub has updated this feature to be usable by PR authors.
Today after making a fork of a public repo that I am in no way affiliated with, I authored a PR and then the reviewer requested changes.
After making the changes, I was able to click the "refresh" icon next to the reviewer to request a review.

GitHub still documents that requesting a review requires write access to the repository. But, on that same page, GitHub also documents the distinct re-review workflow: after someone has reviewed your pull request and you make changes, you can request another review from the same reviewer, using the 🔄 Re-request review control.

That also works in the web UI for an external contributor who opened the PR from a fork and does not have write access to the upstream repository. This was reported in February 2025 in GitHub Community discussion #151024: the external PR author could re-request the review through the web UI, while the equivalent GraphQL and REST API operations failed until the author was made a collaborator.

You can still see that distinction in 2026. github/github-mcp-server issue #3027, opened in August 2026, reproduces it with a public cross-fork PR: the author has no write access to the upstream repository and receives a 404 when requesting the review through the API, while Re-request review succeeds for the same PR through the GitHub web UI.

I could not find a GitHub Changelog entry announcing when that permission distinction was introduced. The original February 2019 GitHub Changelog entry announced the Re-request review feature itself, but did not describe the special case for pull-request authors without write access. I also found no corresponding item in the GitHub public roadmap. The closest, roadmap issue #212, is about restricting who may approve or request changes on pull requests, which is a different permission.

Original answer (2019):

2 years and a half years later, (February 2019), do check if the new button "Re-request review" would help.

As illustrated on twitter, if your PR was already reviewed, but now it’s time for round 2: With fresh eyes and fresh code, re-request a review 🔃

Note/caveat: (from "Requesting a pull request review")

Pull request authors can't request reviews unless they are either a repository owner or collaborator with write access to the repository.

As noted in the comments by gertvdijk:

I am a contributor on the project and the owner of the PR.
It does not make sense to me that I need to be a collaborator on the project to request a re-review?

Oh, wow, it's by design that PR authors can't use this feature?
Damn, that's very much killing the whole feature.

Q: Should we handle all things by plugins and components in october cms? A:

You can override the blog plugins components default markup with your own and add your author information there.

To do that you should learn about overriding plugin components markup here

https://octobercms.com/docs/cms/components#customizing-default-markup

I also think you would benefit by watching this video to help you understand how to use and set up Rainlab's blog plugin.

https://vimeo.com/97088926

Lastly, I dont think you need to use the onEnd() php function. The author/user information is available to you in {{ post }} and can accessed as you mentioned using... 

{{ post.user.first_name }}

Q: Should (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) be 2048.0 or 2049.0? A:

By default, if a target does not support short floating operations natively, std::float16_t maps to the compiler supported __fp16 that is used as a storage format. It is promoted to float as soon as you do calculations on it. Arithmetic operations on __fp16 give float results.

A compiler also may support _Float16 that is as a storage, interchange and arithmetic format. Arithmetic operations on _Float16 give _Float16 results.

Use the compiler flag -fallow-half-arguments-and-returns to map std::float16_t to _Float16 if a target supports _Float16 natively (ARM for example). Note, this breaks the standard ABI.
Just read that -fallow-half-arguments-and-returns is removed, and the mapping std::float16_t to __fp16 or _Float16 depends on compiler target info.

For example, use -march=armv8.2-a+fp16 or -march=armv9-a on ARM and they give the expected result 2048
